opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the two sides really feed into each other. At Princeton, I get to work with students on questions that are a bit longer-horizon: things where we don't know yet whether they'll pan out, like new architectures, or rethinking how attention or state space models should work at a fundamental level. Academia gives you the freedom to explore and to be wrong for a while, which I think is really important.

At Together, I get a very direct view of what actually matters in practice. When you're serving models at scale or helping people train them, you see very quickly where the bottlenecks are: memory bandwidth, inference latency, cost per token. That's incredibly valuable signal. A lot of the problems I end up caring about in research come from seeing those pain points up close.

And it goes the other way too. Some of the ideas we develop in research, things like FlashAttention or work on efficient architectures, can get into production pretty quickly, and then you get feedback on whether they actually hold up on real workloads. That loop is much tighter than if I were only doing one or the other.

So for me it's less about splitting time and more that each side makes the other better. Academia keeps me thinking about the fundamentals, and industry keeps me honest about what actually moves the needle.

r001.rationale: It describes academic work as longer-horizon and Together as providing quick, practical feedback through production workloads and a tighter loop.

r002.rationale: It does not say that academic questions are chosen by anticipating where the world will be in a few years.

r003.rationale: It contrasts academic exploration with practical production concerns, but does not clearly state the distinction between asking whether ideas are interesting and whether startup solutions work and run fast.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two sides really feed each other. At Together, I'm close to the problems that actually matter to people deploying models right now. You see what breaks when you try to serve a model to thousands of users, where the bottlenecks are on real hardware, what inference costs look like at scale. That grounding is incredibly valuable. It keeps me honest about which research directions are actually going to matter versus which ones just look nice on paper.

And then at Princeton, I get to take a longer view. I can work with students on ideas that might take two or three years to pay off, things that no company would prioritize on a quarterly roadmap. A lot of my work, like FlashAttention or the state space model stuff, started from asking fairly fundamental questions about how hardware and algorithms fit together. You need the space to sit with those questions, and academia gives you that.

The other piece is the people. Students bring a kind of fearlessness and fresh perspective that's hard to find anywhere else. And the engineers at Together bring an intensity around making things actually work in production. Being in both worlds means I get the best of both communities, and ideas flow in both directions. Something a student figures out can end up in a production system within months, and a problem we hit in production can turn into a research question for a PhD thesis. That loop is really what I find exciting.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Together’s focus on current deployment needs and quarterly roadmaps with Princeton’s longer view and research ideas that may take two or three years to pay off.

r002.rationale: It describes long-term research, but does not say the questions are chosen by anticipating where the world will be heading in a few years.

r003.rationale: It contrasts research directions that may look good on paper with Together’s focus on making systems work in production, including hardware bottlenecks and inference costs.

astra-6.text:
For me, the two roles complement each other. In academia, you have room to step back and ask longer-term questions, and you get to work with students who bring fresh perspectives. At Together, you see the practical problems that come up when people actually train and deploy models. That helps me think about which research questions could have a meaningful impact.

I like that feedback loop: practical challenges inspire research, and research ideas get tested in real systems. Being able to move between those two environments is a big part of the appeal.

sol-6.1.text:
I like the feedback loop between the two. In academia, you have the freedom to step back and ask longer-term questions, and you get to work with students who bring fresh perspectives. At Together, you see what happens when those ideas meet real workloads: what’s actually slow, what constraints matter, and what people need.

For the kind of research I enjoy—making machine learning more efficient—that connection is really valuable. Practical problems can inspire research questions, and research can turn into something people use. Having both roles lets me stay connected to both sides.
